title: Internal communications videos employees will actually watch
summary: How to turn a CEO memo, weekly update, or org change into a short internal communications video, in several languages, and which tools fit each job.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- Give each internal communications video one job: a leadership update, a weekly bulletin, an all-hands recap, an org-change explainer, or a policy announcement.
- To turn a memo into a video, cut it to the one thing employees must know or do, and show that thing on screen instead of a talking head.
- Aim for 60 to 120 seconds, caption every video, and link the full memo for anyone who wants the detail.
- For several languages, translate the script, voiceover, captions, and on-screen text together, and release every language on the same day.
- Choose the tool by what the video has to show: a recorder for quick personal updates, an avatar generator for presenter-led scripts, a document-to-video platform for memos and decks, and an editor for filmed events.
- Clueso turns a memo, deck, PDF, or script into a narrated, captioned video with motion graphics, and translates it into 150+ languages on every plan, including Free.


You send the reorg memo at 9 AM on Monday. Leadership approved all 900 words of it. By lunch, the same question has landed in your inbox three times, each from someone who stopped reading at the second paragraph.


A memo is the right place to record a decision, but nothing in it tells you who understood the decision. Gallup's US survey for the first half of 2026 found that[49% of employees strongly agree they know what's expected of them at work](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/712433/employee-engagement-remains-flat-adoption-accelerates.aspx) , well below the 61% Gallup measured in 2015. When a reorg or a policy change arrives as a wall of text, the people who skimmed it are the ones left unsure what changed for them.


A short video that puts the new structure on screen, in each employee's own language, answers that question before it reaches your inbox. Making one used to mean a film crew or an editor, which is why most memos never became videos. Clueso, the agentic video platform for businesses, builds the video from the memo you already have: it writes the script, narrates it in an AI voice or your leader's cloned voice, animates the org chart, adds captions, and translates the whole thing into 150+ languages. This guide covers which internal communications videos are worth making, how to turn a memo into one, how to send it in several languages, and which kinds of tools fit which job.


## What is an internal communications video?


An internal communications video is a short video made for employees rather than customers. Common formats are the leadership update, the weekly team bulletin, the all-hands recap, the organizational change explainer, and the policy or benefits announcement. It carries the same message as a memo, but it shows what changed and says it in a voice employees recognize.


Two things set these videos apart from customer-facing ones. Your audience already knows the company, so you can skip the context and open on what changed. And the message usually has a date attached, such as an enrollment window closing or a reporting line changing on the first of the month, so the video has to land before that date.


## Which internal communications videos are worth making?


A video earns its production time when a message goes to most of the company and people need to see something to understand it, like a new structure or a timeline. Everything else can stay an email. Org-change explainers get their own section below, and these formats usually clear the bar too.


### Leadership updates


A quarterly note from the CEO or a function head is the format people most associate with internal video. Keep the leader's own words and, if they're willing, their face for the first 15 seconds. The rest can show the numbers and priorities they're talking about, which spares them a long take.


### Weekly or biweekly updates


A recurring update works when every edition has the same running order and roughly the same length. Employees learn where to find the part that affects them, and your team stops designing each edition from scratch.


### All-hands recaps


The people who missed the meeting are often in another time zone or on shift, and few of them will sit through the hour-long recording. A two-minute recap of the decisions, with a link to the full recording, reaches them.


### Policy and benefits announcements


Policy changes and open enrollment both come with a deadline and an action. A short video that walks through the action and the deadline does more than a PDF attachment, and the PDF stays linked as the reference.


## How do you turn a CEO memo into a short video employees will watch?


Start from the memo rather than a blank page. It already holds the approved wording, and HR or legal may have reviewed it, so the video should stay faithful to it while carrying far less of it.


1. **Write down the one thing each employee should know or do after watching.** If it won't fit in a sentence, the memo holds two announcements and you need two videos.
2. **Cut the script to 60 to 120 seconds.** Read the memo aloud with a timer running first. The video keeps the decision and the next step, and links to the memo for the reasoning.
3. **Decide what's on screen for every line.** Put the new org chart on screen when the script mentions the reorg, and show the date as text when the narration says it.
4. **Open with the leader if they'll appear, then cut to the content.** A few seconds of a real person sets the tone, and their voice can carry the rest over visuals.
5. **Caption everything.** Plenty of employees will play it without headphones, and[WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/captions-prerecorded.html) makes captions on prerecorded video a Level A requirement.
6. **Get the memo's approver to sign off on the script before anyone builds visuals around it.** A line of text takes a minute to change, while a finished edit often has to be rebuilt.


Building the visuals and recording the voiceover take most of the hours, and a tool can draft both for you. Our guide to[turning a PDF or PowerPoint into a video](https://www.clueso.io/blog/turn-pdf-or-powerpoint-into-video) covers the trade-offs.

## How do you explain an organizational change to employees with video?


An org-change announcement can be accurate in every line and still leave people unsure what it means for them. Structure the video around the questions employees ask, in the order they ask them.


1. What is changing, and on what date.
2. Why, in one or two sentences.
3. What stays the same.
4. What each affected group does next, and who to ask.


Show the before and after. A reporting-line change is a diagram, and an animated chart that moves teams from the old box to the new one explains it faster than any paragraph. Clueso builds diagrams like this as[motion graphics](https://www.clueso.io/features/motion-graphics) from a description, so nobody has to animate the boxes by hand.


Send managers the video and the memo first, a day ahead if you can, so they can answer questions when their teams ask. If the change is a new system rather than a new structure, our guide to[rolling out new software with video](https://www.clueso.io/blog/rolling-out-new-software-in-your-tech-stack-win-adoption-with-video) covers the training side.


## How can a small internal comms team produce a weekly video update without a video editor?


Your team will keep a weekly video going only if each edition takes an hour or two. If each one costs a day of someone's week, it won't survive the first busy month.


Fix the format once. Decide the running order, a length cap, and the opening and closing cards, then collect each week's items in one shared doc by a set day. Your team's weekly job is choosing what goes in and getting it approved.


The production side is where a team without an editor needs the tool to do the work. In Clueso, a brand kit on every plan applies your colors, logo, and intro and outro cards to each new video. You paste the week's notes or upload the doc, and Clueso writes the narration, generates the[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) , and adds[captions](https://www.clueso.io/features/video-captions) . Someone on the team reviews the script and the cut before it goes out.


> Start each edition from a reusable[Clueprint](https://www.clueso.io/clueprints) so every weekly update keeps the same layout and pacing.


## How do you send the same announcement in several languages?


Translated captions alone leave employees reading along to a voice in a language they follow less well. For announcements that affect someone's pay or benefits, translate the whole video.


Lock the source script before you translate, because every later edit has to be made once per language. Then work through the rest in order.


- Pick languages from your HR system's location and language data rather than from memory.
- Translate the script, voiceover, captions, and on-screen text together so they agree.
- Keep program names and internal tool names in one approved form across languages.
- Have a fluent colleague review each version for meaning and tone.
- Release every language on the same day, so no office hears the news secondhand.


Clueso translates a finished video into 150+ languages on every plan, including Free. It doesn't translate text inside a screen recording, so if the video shows an internal tool, record the localized version of that screen. ## Frequently asked questions


### What's a good alternative to Synthesia for internal communications videos?


It depends on what the video has to show. If the message needs a presenter on screen in many languages, an avatar-first tool like Synthesia is built for that and is a reasonable choice. If the message is mostly content, such as a new structure or a policy with a deadline, a video that shows that content with motion graphics usually explains it faster than a presenter describing it. Clueso is built for the second case and still includes[AI avatars](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-avatars) , Basic on Free and Solo and Advanced on Business and Enterprise. Our[Clueso vs Synthesia comparison](https://www.clueso.io/vs/synthesia) and[Synthesia alternatives guide](https://www.clueso.io/compare/synthesia-alternatives) go into more detail.


### How long should an internal communications video be?


Aim for 60 to 120 seconds for an announcement, and keep a recap of a longer event to around two minutes with a link to the full recording. If the script runs longer, the video is probably carrying two messages, so split it. In Clueso, you set the length when you convert a document, and the script is drafted to fit it.


### Should we make an AI avatar or a voice clone of our CEO?


Only with the leader's explicit consent, and tell employees when a voice or presenter is synthetic. For personal news, a short phone clip of the real person often lands better than a polished avatar. Clueso's[voice cloning](https://www.clueso.io/features/voice-cloning) and face cloning are on Enterprise and are set up only for someone who has consented, which suits a leader who wants every weekly update, in every language, in their own voice and face without recording each one.


### How do we know whether employees watched?


Compare views against the size of the audience you sent the video to, using the analytics wherever it's hosted. Clueso includes viewership analytics on every plan, so you can see plays and watch time on the intranet page where the video lives.


Open the last all-staff memo that brought the same question back to your inbox more than once. Find the sentence that would have answered it, and make that sentence the first 10 seconds of your next video.
